title: Yield Criteria: Von Mises vs Tresca
text:
In 1d a typical stress-strain figure looks like the following:

This is what experimentalists get when doing a tensile test. After a certain stress \(\sigma_Y\), the behavior of the material is no longer purely elastic and the stress is no longer linearly dependent on the strain. The issue is that in a real material, we do not have uniaxial displacements and stresses, so the stress is a \(3 \times 3\) tensor, but at which stress does it yield? This is where equivalent stress come into play, we use a scalar \(\sigma_{eq} = f(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\) and compare it to the yield stress \(\sigma_Y\) to determine if plastic deformation happen. There are a variety of equivalent stress measures that we can choose, but in this course we consider the Von-Mises and Tresca equivalent stress.
The Von-Mises equivalent stress measures (1.35 in the lecture notes):
\[
\sigma_{eM}(\sigma_{ij}) = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}\sigma_{ij}^\text{dev}\sigma_{ij}^\text{dev}}
\]
One thing that should be noted is that this is a scalar value, and it is an invariant of the stress tensor, meaning that the Von-Mises stress is independent on the basis in which we express the components of the stress tensors. We will see in exercise 5 that the Von-Mises stress can be written in term of principal stress:
\[
\sigma_{vM} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left[(\sigma_1-\sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2-\sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3-\sigma_1)^2\right]}
\]
We also defined the Tresca criterion. \[
\sigma_{\text{Tresca}} = \max\big(|\sigma_1-\sigma_2|,\ |\sigma_2-\sigma_3|,\ |\sigma_3-\sigma_1|\big) = \sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}
\]
In the following cell, you can play around the two criterion and see when they differ.



Deviatoric plane σ₁+σ₂+σ₃ = const, projected orthogonal to the hydrostatic axis (1,1,1)

  
    
      
      
        σ₁ 200
        
      
      
        σ₂ 0
        
      
      
        σ₃ 0
        
      
      
      
        σ_y 200
        
      

      
        Uniaxial tension
        Uniaxial compression
        Pure shear
        Equibiaxial
        Mixed
      

      
        σ_m (hydrostatic)
        σ_vm (Von Mises)
        σ_tresca (σ_max−σ_min)
      
      
    

    
      
      
        Von Mises
        Tresca
        stress state
      
    
  

  
    The two criteria always agree exactly at the hexagon's corners (uniaxial-like states, where two
    principal stresses coincide) and diverge most at the midpoints of the hexagon's edges
    (pure-shear-like states), where Tresca is more conservative by a factor of 2/√3 ≈ 1.155.
    Motion purely along the hydrostatic axis (σ₁=σ₂=σ₃) doesn't move the point in this plane at
    all — both criteria are pressure-independent. Because σ_tresca ≥ σ_vm always, the only possible
    disagreement is Tresca predicting yield first. A stress state far enough out to leave the frame
    is drawn as a hollow marker on the boundary; the readouts stay exact.
  




The two criteria always agree at the hexagon’s corners and diverge most at the edge midpoints (pure-shear states), where Tresca is more conservative by \(2/\sqrt{3}\approx1.155\).

title: Deviatoric / Spherical Decomposition
text:
Consider either the stress or the strain tensor. They can be decomposed into its spherical and volumetric part (Lecture notes 1.15 and 1.16).
\[
\sigma_{ij} = \sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} + \sigma_{ij}^{\text{dev}}
\]
where \(\sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} = \frac{1}{3} \sigma_{kk} \delta_{ij}\) is called the spherical part of the tensor. The deviatoric part is then given by
\[
\sigma_{ij}^{\text{dev}} = \sigma_{ij} - \sigma_{ij}^{\text{sph}} = \sigma_{ij} - \frac{1}{3} \sigma_{kk} \delta_{ij}
\]
In matrix notation:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{13} \\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22} & \sigma_{23} \\
\sigma_{31} & \sigma_{32} & \sigma_{33}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
\sigma_m = \frac{1}{3}\,\text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \frac{1}{3}\left(\sigma_{11}+\sigma_{22}+\sigma_{33}\right)
\]
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{sph} = \sigma_m \, \mathbf{I} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_m & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \sigma_m & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \sigma_m
\end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{dev} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} - \sigma_m \, \mathbf{I} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11}-\sigma_m & \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{13} \\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22}-\sigma_m & \sigma_{23} \\
\sigma_{31} & \sigma_{32} & \sigma_{33}-\sigma_m
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Remark: What is the trace of a deviatoric tensor? Calculate it!


The following interactive illustration computes the deviatoric part and spherical part of the strain (in 2d). Starting from a square, the deformation due to the spherical and deviatoric part of the tensor are shown. Keep the values for \(\epsilon_{11}, \epsilon_{12}\), and \(\epsilon_{22}\) relatively low. What happens to the shape and the deformed area under deviatoric and spherical strain? Push the values for the deformation higher, does it still hold?

The area change is due to the spherical part and the deviatoric part deforms the solid but keeps the area constant. But this only holds for infinitesimal deformation!




ε = εsph + εdev — drag the sliders to set ε₁₁, ε₂₂, ε₁₂

  
    
      ε₁₁ 0.18
      
    
    
      ε₂₂ -0.06
      
    
    
      ε₁₂ = ε₂₁ 0.10
      
    
  

  
    Pure dilation
    Pure deviatoric (equal and opposite)
    Pure shear
    Mixed
    Reset to zero
  

  
    
      
      εsph = εv I — area change, no shape change
      
      
    
    
      
      εdev = ε − εv I — shape change, tr = 0
      
      
    
    
      
      ε = εsph + εdev
      
      
    
  

  
    
      ε
      
    
    
      εsph = εvI, εv = ½tr(ε) in 2D
      
    
    
      εdev (tr = 0)
      
    
  

  
    This is the two-dimensional split, so the spherical part carries εv = ½tr(ε);
    in 3D the same construction uses ⅓tr(ε), and it's a common slip to carry the ½ across.
    Axes are drawn maths-convention (x₁ right, x₂ up), so a positive ε₁₂ tilts the square
    the way it does in a textbook figure. Squares are drawn with the finite map x′ = (I + ε)x for
    visual clarity, not the strict infinitesimal linearization — so at large strain the
    "area-preserving" property of the deviatoric part is only approximate (visible as small drift
    in the reported areas).

    lam = 0. #Write them yourself

    Args:
        lam : First Lamé parameter
        mu : Second Lamé parameter (shear modulus)

    Returns:
        (E, nu): Young's modulus and Poisson ratio.
    """
    E = 0. #Write it yourself

title: Helper functions
text:
Deviatoric and Volumetric part helpers
For convenience, we will write the function in such a way that they can be used for both numpy and sympy computation. To do so, a small trick we use is the following function:

def is_sympy_array(S):
    """
    Check whether S is a sympy matrix/array rather than a numpy array.
    Useful when you want one function to work generically with either
    numeric (numpy) or symbolic (sympy) tensors.
    """
    return isinstance(S, sp.MatrixBase)

We use this function in the way below:

def vol(S):
    """
    Volumetric (spherical) part of a second order tensor.
    vol(S) = tr(S)/3 * I.
    """
    n = S.shape[0]
    if is_sympy_array(S):
        trace = 0. #Write it yourself
        I = 0. #Write it yourself
    else:
        trace = 0. #Write it yourself
        I = 0. #Write it yourself
    return trace * I

def dev(S):
    """
    Deviatoric part of a second order tensor (additive decomposition).
    dev(S) = S - vol(S).
    """
    return 0. #Write it yourself

title: Helper functions
text:
Voigt formulation and elasticity matrix
A very regular thing we do is switching back and forth between the Voigt and Tensor notation for both the stress and the strain. The following helpers function do that. Beforehand, reminder that the Cauchy stress tensor \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) and small strain tensor \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) are symmetric. The following function will be used to check that to prevent input errors.

def check_symmetry(A, tol=1e-10):
    """
    Raise an error if matrix A is not symmetric.

    Parameters
    ----------
    A : array-like or sympy Matrix, shape (n,n)
    tol : float
        Tolerance for numeric comparisons (ignored for symbolic input,
        where equality must hold exactly after simplification).
    """
    symbolic = is_sympy_array(A)

    if symbolic:
        diff = sp.simplify(A - A.T)
        if not diff.is_zero_matrix:
            raise ValueError("Matrix is not symmetric")
    else:
        A = np.asarray(A)
        if A.shape[0] != A.shape[1]:
            raise ValueError("Matrix is not square")
        if not np.allclose(A, A.T, atol=tol):
            raise ValueError("Matrix is not symmetric")







Important



Be mindful of convention when switching back and forth between Voigt and Tensor notation, the shear component have a factor of 2 in the case of strain, but not for the stress!



def stiffness_matrix_voigt(lam, mu) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Isotropic stiffness matrix C_iso in Voigt notation (6x6), engineering shear strain convention.
    sigma = C_iso @ [e11, e22, e33, 2e23, 2e13, 2e12]
    Automatically uses sympy if lam or mu is a sympy expression, else numpy.
    """
    symbolic = isinstance(lam, sp.Basic) or isinstance(mu, sp.Basic)
    C = sp.zeros(6, 6) if symbolic else np.zeros((6, 6))

    C[0, 0] = C[1, 1] = C[2, 2] = 0. #Write it yourself
    C[0, 1] = C[0, 2] = C[1, 0] = C[1, 2] = C[2, 0] = C[2, 1] = 0. #Write it yourself
    C[3, 3] = C[4, 4] = C[5, 5] = 0. #Write it yourself
    return C

def compliance_matrix_voigt(E, nu) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Isotropic compliance matrix S_iso in Voigt notation (6x6), engineering shear strain convention.
    [e11, e22, e33, 2e23, 2e13, 2e12] = S_iso @ sigma
    Automatically uses sympy if E or nu is a sympy expression, else numpy.
    """
    symbolic = isinstance(E, sp.Basic) or isinstance(nu, sp.Basic)
    S = sp.zeros(6, 6) if symbolic else np.zeros((6, 6))

    S[0, 0] = S[1, 1] = S[2, 2] = 0. #Write it yourself
    S[0, 1] = S[0, 2] = S[1, 0] = S[1, 2] = S[2, 0] = S[2, 1] = 0. #Write it yourself
    S[3, 3] = S[4, 4] = S[5, 5] = 0. #Write it yourself

    S = 0. #Write it yourself

    return S

def to_voigt(eps_or_sigma, mode="strain"):
    """
    Convert a symmetric second-order tensor (2x2 or 3x3) to Voigt notation.

    Parameters
    ----------
    eps_or_sigma : array-like or sympy Matrix, shape (2,2) or (3,3)
        Strain or stress tensor.
    mode : str
        "strain" -> off-diagonal terms multiplied by 2 (engineering shear strain)
        "stress" -> off-diagonal terms unchanged

    Returns
    -------
    Voigt vector:
        3x3 input -> shape (6,): [11, 22, 33, 23, 13, 12]
        2x2 input -> shape (3,): [11, 22, 12]
    """
    check_symmetry(eps_or_sigma)
    symbolic = isinstance(eps_or_sigma[0, 0], sp.Basic)
    dim = eps_or_sigma.shape[0]

    if mode == "strain":
        n = 2
    elif mode == "stress":
        n = 1
    else:
        raise ValueError('Unknown mode. Allowed modes are "stress" and "strain"')

    if dim == 3:
        voigt = sp.zeros(6, 1) if symbolic else np.zeros(6)
        voigt[0] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[1] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[2] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[3] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[4] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[5] = 0. #Write it yourself
    elif dim == 2:
        voigt = sp.zeros(3, 1) if symbolic else np.zeros(3)
        voigt[0] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[1] = 0. #Write it yourself
        voigt[2] = 0. #Write it yourself
    else:
        raise ValueError("Input must be a 2x2 or 3x3 tensor")

    return voigt

def from_voigt(voigt, mode="strain"):
    """
    Convert a Voigt-notation vector back to a symmetric second-order tensor.

    Parameters
    ----------
    voigt : array-like or sympy Matrix, length 3 or 6
        length 6 -> [11, 22, 33, 23, 13, 12] -> returns 3x3 tensor
        length 3 -> [11, 22, 12]             -> returns 2x2 tensor
    mode : str
        "strain" -> off-diagonal voigt terms divided by 2 (undo engineering shear strain)
        "stress" -> off-diagonal voigt terms unchanged

    Returns
    -------
    Symmetric tensor, shape (2,2) or (3,3)
    """
    symbolic = isinstance(voigt[0], sp.Basic)
    n_entries = voigt.shape[0] if hasattr(voigt, "shape") else len(voigt)

    if mode == "strain":
        n = 2
    elif mode == "stress":
        n = 1
    else:
        raise ValueError('Unknown mode. Allowed modes are "stress" and "strain"')

    if n_entries == 6:
        T = sp.zeros(3, 3) if symbolic else np.zeros((3, 3))
        T[0, 0] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[1, 1] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[2, 2] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[1, 2] = T[2, 1] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[0, 2] = T[2, 0] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[0, 1] = T[1, 0] = 0. #Write it yourself
    elif n_entries == 3:
        T = sp.zeros(2, 2) if symbolic else np.zeros((2, 2))
        T[0, 0] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[1, 1] = 0. #Write it yourself
        T[0, 1] = T[1, 0] = 0. #Write it yourself
    else:
        raise ValueError("Input must have length 3 or 6")

    return T

title: Problems 1–7: Code and hint
text:
Problem 4






NoteProblem 4



Determine the principal stresses at a point of a linear isotropic elastic material (aluminum) with \(E = 75 \cdot 10^3\) MPa and \(\nu = 0.3\) if the strain components (in a coordinate system) are
\[
[\epsilon_{ij}] =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & 0 & 0.5 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0.5 & 0 & 1.5
\end{bmatrix}
\cdot 10^{-3}
\]


There are two ways to do it, numerically and by hand. First compute the stress like in the previous problem. First, we will compute the stress like in the last problem


Code
eps = np.array([[2,0,0.5],[0,1,0],[0.5,0,1.5]])*1e-3


E = 75e3
nu = 0.3
lam,mu = lambda_mu(E,nu)

C = stiffness_matrix_voigt(lam,mu)

stress_voigt = C@to_voigt(eps,"strain")


stress = from_voigt(stress_voigt,"stress")
sp.Matrix(np.round(stress, 1)) #For pretty printing of output


\(\displaystyle \left[\begin{matrix}310.1 & 0.0 & 28.8\\0.0 & 252.4 & 0.0\\28.8 & 0.0 & 281.2\end{matrix}\right]\)


Then, the principal stresses are the eigenvalues of the stress tensors. The principal stresses are ordered, with \(\sigma_1\) being the largest.


Code
principal_stresses = np.linalg.eigvals(stress)
sp.Matrix(np.sort(principal_stresses)[::-1].round(1)) #[::-1] reverses the array so the first one is the largest


\(\displaystyle \left[\begin{matrix}327.9\\263.4\\252.4\end{matrix}\right]\)


Doing it by hand, we need to find the eigenvalues by finding the root of the characteristic polynomial:
\[
\det(\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda \boldsymbol{I}) = \lambda^3 - I_1\lambda^2 + I_2\lambda - I_3 = 0
\]
\[
I_1 = \text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) = \sigma_{11}+\sigma_{22}+\sigma_{33}
\]
\[
I_2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[(\text{tr}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma})^2 - \text{tr}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^2)\right] = \sigma_{11}\sigma_{22}+\sigma_{22}\sigma_{33}+\sigma_{33}\sigma_{11} - \sigma_{12}^2-\sigma_{23}^2-\sigma_{13}^2
\]
\[
I_3 = \det(\boldsymbol{\sigma})
\]
Small trick: For a isotropic, linear elastic constitutive law the principal directions vector are co-axials. This means that if we express the strain tensor in the principal direction basis, that is
\[
\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \begin{pmatrix}
\epsilon_1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \epsilon_2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \epsilon_3
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Then the resulting stress we get is also expressed in terms of principal stresses:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \sigma_2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \sigma_3
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Given the expressions that we are given for the strain tensor and the stress tensor that we calculated above, which characteristic polynomial do you feel will be easiest to solve by hand? How do you use it to your advantage?

title: Problems 1–7: Code and hint
text:
Problem 5






NoteProblem 5



Derive the explicit expression for the Mises equivalent stress in terms of the principal stresses \(\sigma_1\), \(\sigma_2\) and \(\sigma_3\):
\[
\sigma_{\text{eM}}(\sigma_{ij}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left[(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2 + (\sigma_2 - \sigma_3)^2 + (\sigma_3 - \sigma_1)^2\right]^{1/2}
\]


We first verify that the Von-Mises stress is invariant under a change of basis (You can also take it as granted).






NoteOptional: VM stress is an invariant





To do so, we prove that the double contraction is invariant under a change of basis. Let \(T\) be a second order tensor and \(T'\) the same tensor expressed in a different orthonormal basis. Then, the component of \(T'\) can be written as
\[
T'_{ij} = L_{ik} T_{kl} L_{lj}^T
\]
where \(L\) is an orthogonal tensor so that \(L_{ik}L_{kj}^T = \delta_{ij} = L_{ik}^T L_{kj}\). Then
\[
T'_{ij} T'_{ij} = L_{ik} T_{kl} L_{lj}^T L_{im} T_{mn} L_{mj}^T = T_{kl} T_{mn}  L_{ki}^T L_{im} L_{lj}^T L_{jm}
\]
This gives
\[
T'_{ij} T'_{ij} =  T_{kl} T_{mn} \delta_{km} \delta_{lm} =  T_{mn} T_{mn}
\]
Then, because the trace operator is invariant under a change of basis, it follows that \(T'^{\text{dev}} = T^\text{dev}\).



Then, we write the stress tensor in the principal eigenvector basis so that
\[
\sigma  = \begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & \sigma2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \sigma_3
\end{pmatrix}
\]
so that \(\sigma^{dev} : \sigma^{dev} = (\sigma_i - 1/3 \sigma_{mm}) (\sigma_i -1/3 \sigma_{nn}) = \sigma_i \sigma_i -1/9(\sigma_{mm}\sigma_{nn})\).
You can solve everything by hand, but a simple verification is to write both formula and check that they are equal using sympy. To get rid of the square root we consider the formulas for \(\sigma_{vM}^2\) instead.


Code
s1 , s2 , s3 = sp.symbols("s1,s2,s3")
vM_sq1 = 3/2*(s1**2+s2**2+s3**2 -1/3*(s1+s2+s3)**2) #First formula
vM_sq2  = 1/2*((s1-s2)**2+(s2-s3)**2+(s1-s3)**2) #Second formula
diff = vM_sq1-vM_sq2
sp.simplify(diff)

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
section: Poisson’s ratio — what does it mean?
text:
Poisson’s ratio — what does it mean?
Pull a bar and it usually gets thinner — that lateral response is set by \(\nu\). Try the presets below: cork (\(\nu\approx0\)), typical metals (\(\nu\approx0.3\)), rubber (\(\nu\approx0.499\), nearly incompressible), and auxetic foam (\(\nu<0\), gets fatter when stretched).



Pull a bar along its length — ν sets how much it shrinks (or grows) sideways

  
    
      Applied axial strain ε 0.20
      
    
    
      
      Poisson's ratio ν 0.300
      
    
  

  
    Typical metal (ν≈0.30)
    Cork (ν≈0.00)
    Rubber (ν≈0.499)
    Perfectly incompressible (ν=0.5)
    Auxetic foam (ν≈−0.5)
  

  
    
    
      Axial strain ε
      Lateral strain ε_lat = −νε
      Width W/W₀
      Volume change ΔV/V₀ = (1−2ν)ε
    
  

  
    Pull most ordinary materials and they get thinner as they get longer — that's a positive
    Poisson's ratio. ν=0 means no lateral response at all (like cork, which is why it's easy to push
    into a bottle without swelling out the sides). ν=0.5 means the material can't change volume — it
    must get thinner by exactly the amount needed to conserve volume (rubber, most fluids). Negative ν
    ("auxetic") materials do the opposite of intuition: pull them and they get fatter, not thinner.
    The volume readout is the linearised ΔV/V₀ = tr(ε) = (1−2ν)ε, so ν=0.5 gives exactly zero; the
    drawing stretches the bar by the finite factors (1+ε) and (1+ε_lat), which differ from the
    linearised picture by second-order terms at the large strains these sliders allow.

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
text:
Lamé constants ↔︎ (E, ν)
\[
\mu = \frac{E}{2(1+\nu)}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{E\nu}{(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)}, \qquad K = \frac{E}{3(1-2\nu)}
\]



Live isotropic elasticity conversion and 6×6 Voigt stiffness matrix (order 11,22,33,23,13,12)

  
    
      E (Young's modulus) 70 GPa
      
    
    
      ν (Poisson's ratio) 0.330
      
    
  

  Approaching the incompressible limit (ν → 0.5): λ and K diverge. Common for rubber-like materials; not physical for most metals/alloys.

  
    
      DERIVED CONSTANTS
      
        λ (Lamé's first parameter)
        μ = G (shear modulus)
        K (bulk modulus)
      
      
        μ = E / [2(1+ν)]  ·  λ = Eν / [(1+ν)(1−2ν)]  ·  K = E / [3(1−2ν)] = λ + 2μ/3
      

      λ(ν) AT FIXED E — SINGULARITY AT ν=0.5
      
    

    
      ISOTROPIC STIFFNESS MATRIX C (VOIGT)
      
    
  

  
    C relates Voigt stress and (engineering-shear) strain vectors: σ_V = C·ε_V, with the diagonal shear
    terms equal to μ (not 2μ) because γ_ij = 2ε_ij already carries the factor of two. Off-diagonal 4-5-6
    blocks are zero for an isotropic material — normal and shear response never couple. λ is linear in E
    at fixed ν, so moving the E slider rescales the λ(ν) curve without changing its shape — watch the
    axis numbers, not the outline.

title: Elastic Constants: E, ν, λ, μ
section: What do λ and μ mean physically?
text:
What do λ and μ mean physically?
\(\mu\) resists pure shape change (shear). \(\lambda\) is subtler — it’s the stress that appears sideways only when lateral strain is prevented (confined loading), not something you’d feel in a free pull test.



μ resists shape change; λ is the stress that shows up sideways when shape change is prevented

  
    
      μ (shear modulus) 40 GPa
      
    
    
      λ (Lamé's 1st parameter) 60 GPa
      
    
  

  Unstable isotropic material: stability needs μ > 0 and 3λ+2μ > 0 (i.e. K > 0). Strains are not reported here.

  
    
      μ — resistance to shape change
      Set the shear stress τ; γ = τ/μ is the resulting shear strain
      
      
        Shear stress τ 10.0 GPa
        
      
      γ = τ/μ = 
    

    
      λ — sideways stress when confined
      Set the axial stress σ on a bar between rigid walls (ε_lateral locked at 0); ε_axial = σ/(λ+2μ)
      
      
        Axial stress σ_axial 21 GPa
        
      
      ε_axial = σ/(λ+2μ) = σ_wall = λε = 
    
  

  
    Left: apply a shear stress τ and read off the resulting angle γ = τ/μ — no volume or lateral
    coupling involved, just μ resisting the change of shape. Right: apply an axial stress σ to a bar
    whose sides are clamped so it can't bulge or neck sideways (ε_lateral = 0 by construction,
    not by Poisson relaxation) — the walls still feel a push or pull, and that reaction is exactly λε.
    λ isn't a "stiffness" you can feel directly in an unconstrained pull test (that's E); it only shows
    up once something stops the material from doing what its Poisson's ratio would otherwise let it do.
    Note λ+2μ = M, the constrained (uniaxial-strain) modulus — the same quantity that sets P-wave speed
    in geomechanics/seismology. The outward (green) wall reaction assumes the bar is bonded to
    the walls: a smooth rigid wall can only push, and an unbonded bar under axial compression would
    simply separate from it. Isotropic stability requires μ > 0 and 3λ+2μ > 0; outside that
    window the strain readouts are suppressed rather than shown with a nonsense sign. The drawings
    saturate at a fixed deformation so the figure stays inside its box — the numbers above keep going.
